title: Pattern operates on borrowed USDS: minting draws vault debt and burning wipes it
content:
The mint path in A.6.1.1.6.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.1.1.1 routes through two contracts: the controller "will mint the required USDS into the buffer contract" and then "transfer the newly minted USDS from the buffer to the Proxy." The heading above it is explicit about provenance — the relayer mints USDS "from the Sky Allocation Vault to the Pattern ALM Proxy."

The burn path makes the liability visible. A.6.1.1.6.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.1.2 describes it as returning "and then burn[ing] **Pattern's USDS debt** in the Sky Allocation Vault," and the call "will burn the USDS from the buffer and `wipe` an equivalent amount from the vault's debt."

So Pattern does not hold USDS it owns; it draws on a credit line from Sky, deploys the proceeds into credit markets, and repays by burning. Its economics are those of a leveraged intermediary: earnings are the spread between what its allocations yield and the cost of the vault position, and its solvency question is whether asset value covers vault debt.

This is why so many of the surrounding controls exist and why they belong to Sky rather than to Pattern. The mint rate limit is a credit limit. The Encumbrance Ratio commitment is a leverage covenant. The Freezer's trigger — non-compliance with Risk Capital or Asset Liability Management rules — is a covenant breach. Read through that lens, the Liquidity Layer's permission structure is a lending agreement expressed as smart contract roles.
description: mintUSDS creates USDS in the Allocator Buffer against the Sky Allocation Vault before it reaches the ALM Proxy, so the Agent's working capital is a liability to Sky rather than owned funds.
